extracted.intended_audience: People of the State of New York; citizens and voters considering ratification of the proposed U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Newspaper essays (Federalist Papers Nos. 27–29) arguing constitutional principles governing standing armies, the militia, and the allocation of military power. The text defends specific structural restraints and arrangements to secure liberty while enabling public order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit military appropriations to two-year periods
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution's provision 'for restraining the appropriations of money for military purposes to the period of two years.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This forces the legislature, 'once at least in every two years, to deliberate upon the propriety of keeping a military force on foot,' requiring a new formal vote and public accountability; it prevents vesting the executive with permanent funds for an army and creates regular opportunities for opposition and state-level vigilance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biennial legislative accountability for maintaining an army
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislature will be obliged at least every two years to deliberate and declare by formal vote whether to keep up a military force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular reconsideration serves as check on expansions of military force: opposition parties and state legislatures can rouse public attention; repeated votes make progressive augmentation and secret conspiracies difficult to sustain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer measured constitutional provisions over absolute prohibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid aiming at 'too much' (e.g., absolute interdictions) which may be ineffective; instead adopt provisions compatible with exigencies and prudence (the two-year appropriation is offered as such).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extreme prohibitions (e.g., total bans phrased as 'SHALL NOT BE kept up') may become mere admonitions or be easily circumvented; measured restraints are more likely to be effective in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: National regulation of the militia to achieve uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformity in organization and discipline of the militia 'would be attended with the most beneficial effects' and can only be accomplished by confiding regulation to the national authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-regulated, uniformly disciplined militia enables mutual intelligence and concert when called into service and reduces the need for a standing army.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve to the states appointment of officers and training authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan empowers the Union 'to provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining the militia, and for governing such part of them as may be employed in the service of the United States, RESERVING TO THE STATES RESPECTIVELY THE APPOINTMENT OF THE OFFICERS, AND THE AUTHORITY OF TRAINING THE MILITIA ACCORDING TO THE DISCIPLINE PRESCRIBED BY CONGRESS.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This balance preserves state involvement and local control (appointment & training) while achieving national uniformity of discipline through congressional prescription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the militia to avoid reliance on standing armies
rubrics_metrics.description: If the federal government can command the militia in emergencies, it will have less occasion to recur to a regular standing army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empowering the Union to call and regulate the militia is a means to render a permanent army unnecessary and so guards against the dangers associated with standing peacetime armies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionate use of force (means proportioned to mischief)
rubrics_metrics.description: In emergencies 'the means to be employed must be proportioned to the extent of the mischief.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small commotions should be handled by the militia; large insurrections or interstate exigencies may require regular troops. The rule emphasizes restraint and appropriateness of the military response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend federal authority to individuals to facilitate ordinary enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Extending federal authority 'to the individual citizens of the several States' enables the government to employ ordinary magistracy in executing laws, reducing reliance on force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporating state magistrates and making federal laws 'the supreme law of the land' binds state officers by oath and creates routine enforcement channels that lessen the need for extraordinary coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual checks between state and federal governments as security
rubrics_metrics.description: State legislatures and the federal government will be 'auxiliary' to each other and mutually capable of checking encroachments, with the people able to throw support into either scale to oppose usurpation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existence of separate state governments and the ability of the people to appeal to them creates continual vigilance and resources to resist federal overreach, making schemes to concentrate military power harder to sustain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic extent and larger union as protection against usurpation
rubrics_metrics.description: The great extent of the country is 'a further security'—an ambitious federal usurpation would face geographic and logistical obstacles and the capacity of distant states to raise opposing forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Size of the republic, together with state-level resistance and the difficulties of sustaining large standing forces across an extensive territory, reduces the likelihood that the federal government could erect a lasting despotism.
